title: Synchronization Primitives in Hardware
summary: The atomic instructions — test-and-set, compare-and-swap, LL/SC — that every lock and lock-free data structure is ultimately built from.

slides.sectionTitle: Why ordinary loads/stores can't build a lock
slides.markdown:
A lock needs to **check whether it's free and grab it** as one indivisible step. If "check" and "grab" are two separate ordinary instructions, two cores can both check, both see it free, and both grab it — a **race** that defeats the entire purpose of a lock.

```
if (lock == FREE) {   // both cores see FREE
  lock = TAKEN;       // both cores set it — both think they won
}
```

This is exactly why hardware provides **atomic read-modify-write** instructions — the check-and-grab has to happen as one uninterruptible operation, or the race is unavoidable.

**Test-and-set** is the earliest atomic primitive: it reads a memory location's old value and unconditionally writes a new value (typically 1/"locked"), returning the old value — all as one atomic step. A core acquires the lock by test-and-setting until it reads back a 0 (was free).

Its weakness is **busy-waiting cost**: every failed attempt still hammers the same memory location with a write, generating heavy coherence traffic ([cache-coherence-protocols](cache-coherence-protocols)) as every spinning core invalidates every other spinning core's cached copy, over and over.

**Compare-and-swap (CAS)** is the workhorse behind most modern lock-free code: atomically compare a memory location's current value against an *expected* value, and only if they match, swap in a *new* value — reporting success or failure. Unlike test-and-set, CAS lets a thread build "update this value, but only if nobody else changed it since I last read it" — the basis for optimistic, retry-based lock-free algorithms.

A typical CAS loop reads the current value, computes a new one, then CAS-swaps; on failure (someone else won the race), it just re-reads and retries rather than blocking.

**Load-linked/store-conditional (LL/SC)** is the alternative many RISC-style ISAs (RISC-V, older MIPS, ARM's LDXR/STXR) use instead of a single CAS instruction: `LL` reads a value and marks the address as watched; `SC` writes a new value **only if no other core has written to that address since the LL** — otherwise it fails and software retries.

LL/SC splits CAS's single atomic instruction into a pair, easier to implement correctly in hardware, at the cost of needing careful handling around interrupts and context switches.

![A CAS-based spinlock's acquire and release sequence across two contending threads](assets/cas-spinlock.svg)

Acquiring: loop calling CAS(lock, expected=0, new=1) until it succeeds — the thread that flips the lock from 0 to 1 wins; every failing thread just retries. Releasing: a plain store of 0 — no atomicity needed, since only the current holder ever writes it, and everyone spinning is only reading.

slides.sectionTitle: CAS vs LL/SC and the ABA problem
slides.markdown:
| | CAS | LL/SC |
|---|---|---|
| Instruction shape | One atomic instruction | A load/store pair |
| ABA problem | **Vulnerable** — value A→B→A looks unchanged to a plain value compare | **Naturally immune** — SC fails if *any* write touched the address, even one that restored the same value |
| Hardware complexity | Higher (one instruction does compare+swap atomically) | Lower per-instruction, but needs careful monitor/reservation hardware |

**How to decide:** CAS alone can be fooled by the **ABA problem** — a value changes from A to B and back to A, and a plain CAS sees no difference even though something happened in between (a classic issue for lock-free stacks); LL/SC sidesteps this because SC tracks *any write to the address*, not just the final value, though real ISAs still often add a version/tag to CAS-based code to get the same protection.
